title: Health Checks and Load Balancing
description: Learn to implement health checks and load balancing for resilient microservices.

data.text: Health checks and load balancing are critical for service reliability. Amazon and Netflix discovered that without proper health checking, load balancers would route traffic to failing instances, causing cascading failures and poor user experiences.

data.title: Health Check Types
items: Liveness: Is the service running? (restart if failing)
Readiness: Is the service ready to accept traffic? (remove from load balancer if failing)
Startup: Has the service finished starting? (prevent traffic during initialization)

data.text: Health checks are usually simple HTTP endpoints that return 200 OK when the service is healthy. They should check critical dependencies like database connections and external APIs, but keep them fast to avoid false positives.

data.title: Health Check Anti-Patterns
data.text: Avoid checking everything in your health endpoint. A slow health check can trigger false positives. Keep it under 5 seconds and check only critical dependencies.

items.question: How often should I run health checks?
items.answer: Every 10-30 seconds is typical. More frequent checks catch failures faster but increase load. Less frequent checks may miss transient failures.

items.question: Should health checks check the database?
items.answer: Yes, but keep it simple. A SELECT 1 query is sufficient. Complex checks can cause false positives and slow down the endpoint.

items.question: What is a load balancer?
items.answer: A load balancer distributes incoming traffic across multiple service instances. It can be hardware (F5), software (NGINX), or cloud-based (AWS ELB).

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Health checks keep load balancers accurate
Use liveness, readiness, and startup probes
Keep health checks fast and simple
Load balancers remove unhealthy instances automatically
data.takeaway: Robust health checks and load balancing are the foundation of reliable microservices.
